editorNote: An Extra Edition week: GNU is announced as Atari’s unwanted cartridges head into a New Mexico landfill, two visions of software’s future arriving within twenty-four hours.
morningLine: A free Unix-compatible system is proposed, Atari buries surplus stock, and Apple cuts the Lisa by $3,000.

lead.headline: Atari Dumps Truckloads of Games in New Mexico Landfill
lead.dek: Cartridges and equipment from the El Paso plant are crushed and buried as the console market’s inventory crisis becomes impossible to hide.
body: Truckloads of Atari material rolled into the Alamogordo, New Mexico, municipal landfill this week, where workers crushed and buried cartridges and equipment shipped from the company’s El Paso plant. A September 28 New York Times brief fixed the disposal to this week, turning a grim inventory operation into the sharpest picture yet of the videogame business’s retreat.

The dumping followed a bruising year for the console trade. Retail shelves had filled with more cartridges than buyers wanted, price-cutting deepened, and Atari’s once-dominant position was squeezed by both home computers and a flood of uneven software. Whatever individual titles lay beneath the soil, the convoy itself testified to the cost of excess stock.

Atari described the buried goods as discarded material, but the scale invited rumor almost immediately. Later archaeological work would confirm that cartridges and hardware were among the debris. The contemporary record supports the central fact without relying on the legends that grew around it: Atari sent truckloads from El Paso to be destroyed in Alamogordo.

For computer and game shops, the lesson was immediate. Software could no longer be treated as an endlessly expanding aisle, and brand recognition could not rescue every cartridge. This week’s landfill scene marks the crash not as an abstraction on a balance sheet, but as physical goods reduced to rubble.

stories.headline: GNU Call Asks Programmers to Build a Free Unix-Compatible System
stories.dek: Richard Stallman names GNU — ‘Gnu’s Not Unix’ — and invites a network of programmers to help create a complete shareable operating system.
body: On September 27, MIT programmer Richard Stallman posted a startling proposal to the net.unix-wizards and net.usoft groups: he intended to write a complete Unix-compatible software system and give it away so that users could share and change it. He named the project GNU, a recursive abbreviation for “Gnu’s Not Unix.”

The plan reached far beyond a single utility. Stallman listed a kernel, editor, shell, C compiler, linker, assembler, formatter, spreadsheet and documentation among the pieces required. Compatibility with Unix would make the system familiar and portable while avoiding dependence on proprietary Unix source.

The announcement asked programmers for contributions of machines, money and code, but its larger claim concerned control: people using computers should be able to study, improve and redistribute the programs on which they depended. That invitation begins a project whose tools and principles will reshape software development.

stories.headline: Apple Cuts Lisa to $6,995 and Points Dealers Toward Macintosh
stories.dek: The pioneering graphical workstation loses $3,000 from its original price while Apple previews a smaller January machine near $2,500.
body: Apple told dealers that a stripped-down Lisa configuration would sell for $6,995, down from the original $9,995. The reduction acknowledged the difficulty of selling an advanced graphical office system at five figures; period reporting put Lisa sales at only about 6,000 units.

The company was already pointing toward its next answer. Time reported that Macintosh was planned for a January introduction around $2,500, bringing Lisa-derived graphical ideas to a much broader price bracket. The cheaper machine was not expected initially to run Lisa or IBM PC software, making its ease of use central to Apple’s gamble.

IBM’s advance was the pressure behind the reset. Dataquest figures cited in the same report put IBM ahead of Apple in the $1,000-to-$5,000 segment, reversing their positions from the previous December.

stories.headline: IBM’s Unannounced ‘Peanut’ Has the Home Market Guessing
stories.dek: Before IBM confirms a name, price or specification, expectations for its home computer are already moving the market.
body: A September 27 New York Times personal-computing column captured the industry’s fixation on IBM’s rumored low-cost “Peanut.” Dealers and competitors expected a machine aimed at homes, but IBM had not announced it, leaving every price and specification in the realm of informed speculation.

The rumor mattered because IBM’s entry could reset expectations for Apple, Commodore, Atari, Tandy and Coleco. Buyers faced a familiar choice: purchase a proven machine now or wait for the weight of the IBM name. Until an official unveiling, the most important fact about Peanut was the pressure created simply by its possibility.
